inline.s: Dharmas arise from conditions; speaking too arises from conditions; and the speaker of Dharma likewise arises from conditions. Since it is said to be condition-arisen, it is not that there is no Dharma, not that there is no speaking, not that there is no speaker of Dharma. Yet what arises from conditions has no own-nature; its very substance is empty. Hence although there is plainly a speaker of Dharma, at the very moment he is speaking with full intensity and Dharma is plainly present, it is at once utterly ungraspable. This is what is meant by “nothing spoken.” It means that his speaking is no speaking. If one supposes there is something spoken, one does not know it to be condition-arisen, and clings to it as real. Once one understands the meaning of condition-arising, one knows that Dharma is fundamentally without Dharma, and so speaking is no speaking. Even the speaker of Dharma is at once empty and at once provisional, at once provisional and at once empty. One will never recklessly fabricate words and thoughts, committing an offense equal to slandering the Buddha. As for why ordinary beings recklessly fabricate words and thoughts: their fundamental error is nothing but supposing that since there is a speaker of Dharma, there must be a Dharma spoken. If no Dharma were spoken, there would be no speaker of Dharma. The Tathāgata comes into the world precisely to speak Dharma and save beings — is there not plainly a speaker of Dharma? So they rashly say the Tathāgata has something spoken. This is to fail utterly to understand the meaning of the three bodies, mistaking the dharma-body for one that speaks. (The dharma-body does not speak; only the reward-body and transformation-body speak.) They further suppose that since he speaks Dharma, there must be a thought of speaking Dharma. If there were no thought of speaking Dharma, how could he speak? So they rashly say: the Tathāgata gives rise to the thought, “I should speak Dharma.” This again fails utterly to understand that it is precisely because of no-thought and empty stillness that he can speak Dharma. Hence the text says not only that there is no Dharma that can be spoken, but that the speaker of Dharma has no Dharma that can be spoken. The two sentences joined together are exactly what breaks their ordinary sentiment. Why? Since the speaker of Dharma has no Dharma that can be spoken, it is clear he cannot be clung to as a speaker of Dharma. And if there is not even a Dharma that can be spoken, how could there be a thought of speaking? Yet plainly there is a speaker of Dharma, plainly there is Dharma to speak — what of that? You must realize: this is merely named speaking Dharma. “Named” means provisionally named. You should know that because it is a provisional name for speaking Dharma, although he is named a speaker of Dharma there is no harm in no Dharma being speakable; and although no Dharma is speakable, there is no harm in his being named a speaker of Dharma. You should further know that the reason the provisionally named speaker of Dharma has no Dharma that can be spoken is precisely that, because no Dharma can be spoken, there come to be the provisional names of speaking Dharma and of a speaker of Dharma. (Because of emptiness and no-thought, the two knowledges are accomplished, and one can speak all kinds of Buddha-Dharma. As quoted earlier from the Sutra of Golden Light.) If you understand this meaning, doubting thoughts and reckless words need not arise, and the offense of slandering the Buddha may be escaped. It was said above: in this sutra, every phrase “is named” should be understood as a provisional name, and must not be taken as literal fact. Looking at the earlier phrase “is named the mind,” this should now be perfectly clear. And the phrase here, “is named speaking Dharma,” proves it still further. For if one takes it literally and says, “This is what is called speaking Dharma,” then there is something spoken. If one sentence is like this, every sentence is like this. One absolutely must not take them literally and pin them down.

The positive meaning has now been fully set forth. You should know that this great division on opening the Buddha’s knowing and seeing is entirely spoken so as to cause those who are awakened to penetrate its principle and remove their self-view. Therefore the words here, “do not give rise to such a thought,” are an admonition that a bodhisattva should not give rise to thought. “Do not say the Tathāgata gives rise to the thought, ‘I should…’” makes clear that even speaking Dharma should not involve a thought — how much less anything else. Moreover it causes one to contemplate that the nature of true suchness is originally without thought, and thus to contemplate that all dharmas are of the meaning of suchness, emptiness and existence perfectly interfused. The words “then one slanders the Buddha and does not understand what is spoken” make clear that if one gives rise to thought at all, one contravenes the Buddha’s intent. If one says the Buddha has a Dharma that is spoken, is that not a dharma-nature not yet purified? In short, the meaning of neither one nor different is not yet clear. Though one hears Buddha-Dharma, one will surely find it hard to grasp. One will inevitably cling to existence and doubt emptiness, or cling to emptiness and doubt existence, misleading Dharma and misleading people, committing offenses without knowing it. Therefore the first essential in studying the Buddha’s teaching lies in seeing perfectly and knowing rightly — what is called opening one’s understanding. Hence he further reveals the meaning that the speaker of Dharma has no Dharma that can be spoken, which is named speaking Dharma, so that they may comprehend and penetrate it. If one knows that the Dharma the Buddha speaks is fundamentally without Dharma, one knows that all dharmas are exactly like this.

When you know that Dharma, speech, and the speaker of Dharma are all condition-arisen, at once empty and at once provisional, at once provisional and at once empty, named yet without reality, then you know that all worldly and transcendental dharmas, all speech, and all students of Dharma are exactly like this. Since the speaker of Dharma has no Dharma that can be spoken, the student of Dharma naturally has no Dharma that can be clung to. Since the speaking of Dharma is without thought, the student of Dharma should contemplate that all dharmas, being condition-arisen, are empty in substance, and converge into one suchness. As the power of contemplation gradually deepens, discrimination and attachment gradually thin, self-view is gradually removed, and thought too is gradually left behind. This is what is meant by “one who penetrates the dharma of no-self” — just so, just so. A bodhisattva should know it thus. This has been the first statement of the purport of there being no Dharma that can be spoken.
What follows explains the intent behind adding the next subdivision, (Ji) second, making clear that the hearer is empty by nature.

The text of this section was originally absent from Master Kumārajīva’s translation; it was added by later people on the basis of the Wei translation. The first to add it was Master Kuiji in Tang times, but the assembly did not follow him. That it became the accepted version, one voice raising and all responding, began with Master Daoyong’s stone engraving in Southern Tang. Some say it was added by imperial order in the second year of Changqing under Emperor Muzong of Tang — this is wrong. Liu Gongquan copied this sutra in the fourth year of Changqing; Liu was a court official, and if the imperial addition had come two years earlier, why would it be absent from Liu’s text? The Song-era Changshui Record of Determining the Text says: “In the recent editions we now see, this passage is present.” These words suffice as proof that it was first added in Southern Tang; the early Song was close in time to Southern Tang, hence “recent editions.” What was the intent of adding it? Because the Treatise of Asaṅga and Maitreya’s verses both contain this meaning. Yet to say the Qin translation omitted the meaning of the threefold circle being empty seems not entirely so. For the earlier text already has the passage: “a bodhisattva, for the benefit of all living beings, should thus practice giving; the Tathāgata says all marks are no marks; and again he says all living beings are no living beings.” The Qin translation perhaps took the marks of the giver and the given to be included within “all marks are no marks,” and joined to “living beings are no living beings” this suffices to show the threefold circle as empty. Hence it omitted the passage on living beings here, the better to reveal the meaning that both the subject and the object are extinguished. For the words above, “the speaker of Dharma has no Dharma that can be spoken,” clarify that the speaker is empty; and the words below, “no Dharma can be attained,” clarify that what is spoken is empty. When the work of cultivation reaches its utmost, both subject and object must be empty before the light of the nature can shine alone and one is utterly freed from the sense-faculties and their objects. This meaning is exactly what the Heart Sutra states: “no wisdom and also no attainment.” The Qin translation deliberately omitted it, in order to reveal the ultimate accomplishment of progressive practice; it was by no means an omission. Kumārajīva’s translation is meticulous in every character — why would he alone omit this meaning? Nevertheless, with this section the meaning becomes more complete, and its omission in the Qin translation is unavoidably one flaw in a thousand refinements. Therefore in this revised edition everything follows the Tang manuscript sutras, and this section alone follows Daoyong’s stone engraving — for this reason. I should now explain in detail why it ought to be added.

In the early Qing, Master Datian composed the New Eye Commentary, dividing the sutra text into four great divisions: faith, understanding, practice, and realization — because the sutra text plainly possesses this meaning. For instance, in the division on generating faith, the Elder solemnly asks whether there are living beings who can generate true faith; the Buddha likewise solemnly answers that those who observe precepts and cultivate merit can generate faith. And at the end of the division he concludes: “the Buddha and the Dharma of supreme enlightenment all come forth from this sutra.” To say they come forth from this sutra is to point out that students should enter through this sutra. Faith is the gate of entering the Way, and so at the close of this division he draws out this meaning.

In the division on opening understanding, he speaks at length of the fruit and the practice in order to illuminate the causal mind. The Elder himself declares his profound understanding of the purport of the meaning; this is precisely to show people that they should understand profoundly in the same way. The Buddha then confirms and unfolds it in detail, concluding: “you should know that the sutra’s meaning and its reward are both inconceivable.” “You should know” means you should understand — thus he concludes the meaning of profound understanding.

In this division on progressive practice, he first clarifies that the resolve for bodhi is without Dharma, and next causes the opening of the Buddha’s knowing and seeing. The Buddha’s seeing is not clinging to one or different; the Buddha’s knowing is that the mind of the three periods is ungraspable and that all dharmas are originally unborn. And at the point of conclusion he again states plainly: “by means of no-self, no person, no being, and no life, cultivating all good dharmas, one then attains anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.” He further says: “good dharmas are then no good dharmas.” This points out to students that they should penetrate inner mind and outer objects as at once existent and at once empty, not clinging to one or different, without self and without Dharma, as the one and only work of cultivation. The meaning is still more evident. For one must cultivate the cause of no-self and no-Dharma before one can realize the fruit of the equal dharma-realm.

Hence in the fourth great division he states plainly that in all dharmas there is no self, and one accomplishes patience. “Accomplishing patience” is what is called realization. All the rest that is spoken concerns the meaning that in the equal dharma-realm all dharmas are empty in mark, and all of it is the meaning of accomplishment and realization. Faith, understanding, practice, and realization — the sutra text and the sutra’s meaning are plain and evident, complete and ready at hand. That the New Eye Commentary alone perceived this is something no commentator before had ever done; that its commentary is named “New Eye” is indeed no idle claim. Therefore this division and judgment follows it, only adding two general headings — “in terms of mind, clarifying non-abiding” and “in terms of objects, clarifying non-abiding” — to grasp the guiding principles, so that the differing senses of the former and latter halves may be seen at a glance.

You should know that the Avataṃsaka Sutra displays the perfectly interfused and unobstructed stages of entering the Way by means of faith, understanding, practice, and realization. That sutra was spoken when the Buddha had first accomplished the Way, as he empowered the great bodhisattvas and together with them spoke of the state the Tathāgata himself had realized. That state is precisely that all dharmas are one suchness and that all is so. (That he does not speak it himself displays that the dharma-body does not speak.) This Vajra Prajñā was spoken to keep the Buddha-seed unbroken; therefore it is taught entirely according to the Avataṃsaka’s stages of entering the Way by faith, understanding, practice, and realization, so that hearers too may enter the Way by these perfectly interfused stages, thereby showing the meaning of the robe and bowl handed down in succession and lamp lighting lamp without end. That the New Eye Commentary brought out this guiding eye is precisely wherein its excellence lies. Now faith, understanding, practice, and realization are indeed the steps of entering the Way; yet the word faith is especially essential — from beginning to end, it is only a mind of faith. How could faith be merely the gate of entering the Way? The Avataṃsaka Sutra says: “Faith is the mother of the source of the Way and of merits; it nourishes and grows all roots of goodness.” All roots of goodness depend on it for their nourishment; hence in every matter and every dharma one cannot depart from the word faith. Even in this sutra it plainly says: “when the mind of faith is pure, then true marks arise.” This suffices to show that the one word faith runs through to the very bottom. Therefore, since the Buddha has revealed how to have faith, how to understand, how to practice, and how to realize, hearers should one and all give rise to a mind of faith, and likewise so believe, likewise so understand, likewise so practice, likewise so realize. Otherwise they are like one counting another’s treasure, with not half a coin for himself.

Consider the division on generating faith: having said that observing precepts and cultivating merit can generate faith, and that this is to be taken as real, in answer to the Elder’s question, it further says: “one in whom a single thought of pure faith arises gains immeasurable merit and virtue.” This is precisely to encourage those who hear that faith can be generated to arouse faith and observe precepts and cultivate merit, so that they may generate true and pure faith. In the passage on opening understanding, after the profound understanding of the purport, faith is spoken of still more. For example: “when the mind of faith is pure, then true marks arise”; “to believe, understand, receive, and uphold is the very rarest”; “where the mind of faith does not oppose it, the merit surpasses that”; “the mind becomes wild and confused, doubting and not believing.” To speak thus over and again is entirely to display the essentiality of profound understanding. It is also what awakens students to generate faith in the meaning made clear in the division on opening understanding, and to seek to open just such a profound understanding. Opening understanding is clarifying the principle. Only when the principle is clear are faith true and practice solid, and only then may realization be hoped for. Otherwise one believes blindly and practices blindly, wasting one’s effort. That is why faith is spoken of most in this division. In the fourth, on accomplishing realization, there are likewise the words “should thus know, thus see, thus believe and understand,” to show that the Tathāgata’s equal dharma-realm is fundamentally beyond the reach of ordinary beings’ conceptions, and can by no means be measured by ordinary sentiment; only by firm faith can one accord with it and enter. From this we see that in the three great divisions of faith, understanding, and realization, the word faith is in each case specially marked out as the guiding eye, and the division on progressive practice should not alone be lacking it. Yet the Qin translation alone has not a single word of faith in this division. Therefore one should cite the words on faith from the Wei translation of this division and supply them to the Qin translation, to serve as the guiding eye that awakens students, so that they know that all the methods of progressive practice revealed in this division should be deeply believed and practiced in accordance with. Nor is that all. The earlier text’s “marks are no marks” and “living beings are no living beings,” though sufficient to show the threefold circle as empty, yet this passage also says “is named,” showing at once emptiness and at once the provisional. The meaning is more complete. Hence although the earlier text exists, there is no objection to repetition. For the earlier text says only “are not,” which clarifies that giving should not abide in marks; this text also says “is named,” which clarifies that the Dharma-gift and living beings are both condition-arisen dharmas — at once empty and at once provisional, one should give without abiding in marks; at once provisional and at once empty, one should give yet not abide in marks. Hence it is not repetition. Furthermore, as to the meaning that all dharmas are condition-arisen: if there were only the two divisions on merit and on the surpassing reward, without clarifying the meaning in terms of giving, there would be only a teaching in terms of fruit and none in terms of cause, and the meaning would be somewhat incomplete. And clarifying the meaning in terms of the threefold circle being empty already includes the meaning that both subject and object are extinguished. For the giver and the given Dharma are indeed subject and object set against each other; and the person who gives Dharma and the living beings who hear it are likewise subject and object set against each other. Hence to speak of the threefold circle being empty in no way conflicts with the meaning that both subject and object are extinguished. But if one clarifies only that both subject and object are extinguished, it does not include the threefold circle being empty. That is why in this division alone he did not follow the original text but added it — for this reason.
(Ji) Second, clarifying that the hearer is empty by nature. This has three parts: (Wu) first, the question; next, dispelling clinging; third, explaining and establishing.
(Wu) First, the question.
Then Elder Subhūti, rich in wisdom-life, said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, will there be living beings in future ages who, hearing this Dharma spoken, generate a mind of faith?”

“Then” means at the moment the preceding section had just concluded. “Wisdom-life” is an alternative translation of “Elder”; in Tang times it was rendered “full of years,” a different name with the same meaning — both are titles for one advanced in years and rich in virtue. The Qin translation preferred the old terms and so rendered it “Elder”; the Tang translations preferred new coinages and called him “full of years,” to convey the sense that both life and wisdom-life are complete. The Wei translation has “wisdom-life,” a name that seems to speak of only one side; yet to say that wisdom refers to the dharma-body and life covers both life and wisdom-life is not unacceptable either. “Will there be” expresses the fear that there may not be many. The Elder means that in the present there may perhaps be some, but living beings of the future, further from the Buddha, with deep karma and heavy obstruction, may not be many. Hence he says “in future ages.” “This Dharma” broadly gathers all that was said above, from no Dharma for resolving the mind up to no Dharma that can be spoken. He means that in resolving the mind and cultivating practice one must rely on Dharma; now it is said there is no Dharma, and further that the speaker of Dharma has no Dharma that can be spoken — yet all such various statements are themselves Dharma. Beings of the final age, hearing this, will deeply fear doubt; hence he asks: “hearing this Dharma spoken, will they generate a mind of faith?” You should know that all that has been said above is the wondrous Dharma of not clinging to dharmas and earnestly cultivating no-self. The Elder’s question is precisely to point out to students that they should believe this wondrous Dharma and cultivate the practice of no-self.
(Wu) Next, dispelling clinging.
The Buddha said: “Subhūti, they are not living beings, yet not non-living beings.”

The word “they” refers to the living beings who hear the Dharma. “Not living beings” is spoken in terms of nature; “not non-living beings” is spoken in terms of marks. The sense is: shall we call them not living beings? Yet they are not non-living beings. Shall we call them not non-living beings? Yet they are not living beings. This precisely reveals the meaning that they are at once empty and at once provisional, at once provisional and at once empty, and that all living beings are condition-arisen.
(Wu) Third, explaining and establishing.
“Why is this? Subhūti, living beings, living beings — the Tathāgata says they are not living beings; therefore they are named living beings.”

This section explains why it was said above that they are not living beings and not non-living beings. That “living beings, living beings” is said twice continues the preceding “not living beings, not non-living beings.” “The Tathāgata says” means he speaks in terms of nature. “Named” refers to name and mark. The sense is: what was just said, that they are not living beings and not non-living beings, is spoken in terms of nature — they inherently possess the Buddha-nature and are not living beings, hence “they are not living beings”; but in terms of name and mark they are living beings, hence “they are not non-living beings.” Joined with the preceding section, this section’s words are utterly perfect and wondrous and its meaning utterly deep and far-reaching. Let me now set it out in three layers.

(1) The Elder asked whether living beings who hear such a Dharma can generate faith; yet the reply speaks solely in terms of living beings and says not a word on the matter of generating faith. Is this not an answer that does not meet the question? In fact it is not so; the sense of the question has already been perfectly answered. It is, so to speak, an answer by not answering. Why do I say this? The Elder feared that living beings might fail to generate faith in so profound a Dharma because they take living beings to be living beings, and so he could not help worrying on their behalf. Yet this is a mistake: it is to cling to marks and be blind to nature. You should know that viewed in terms of marks, they are indeed living beings, yet it is no more than a provisional name for what is condition-arisen. What is condition-arisen is not nature; their nature is equal to that of all Buddhas and is fundamentally not that of living beings. Since they possess the Buddha-nature, how could they fail to open the Buddha’s right knowing? Then how could those who hear this Dharma be incapable of faith? Hence the single phrase “not living beings, not non-living beings” contains within it the sense: do not speak thus.

(2) The Buddha’s speaking of this section is no different from teaching living beings a skillful means for generating faith upon hearing the Dharma. What is the skillful means? First, contemplate that one’s own body is such. All living beings should contemplate that these many dharmas of the five aggregates come together only through causes and conditions, are not born yet illusorily born, and are originally unborn. If one knows this meaning, one can naturally generate faith in the meaning set forth above: that all dharmas are condition-arisen, at once empty and at once provisional, at once provisional and at once empty, and that in resolving the mind and cultivating practice there is no Dharma that can be clung to. You should know that if the speaker of Dharma has no Dharma that can be spoken, how could one who resolves the mind and cultivates practice in reliance on Dharma have any Dharma to cling to?

(3) In revealing how one who benefits living beings by practicing the six pāramitās of giving should be at once in marks and apart from marks. For “not non-living beings” causes one to realize that living beings, being condition-arisen, are at once provisional and not without their name, and that one should give while dwelling on nothing. This is why it was said earlier that all living beings without exception should be brought to extinction and enter nirvāṇa without residue — the bodhisattva should arouse this great compassion. “Not living beings” causes one to realize that living beings, being condition-arisen, are at once empty and originally not living beings, and that one should give yet not abide in marks. This is why it was said earlier that although all living beings have been brought to extinction, not one living being has actually been brought to extinction — the bodhisattva should possess this great wisdom. In short, the meaning of condition-arising runs through everything. If one can believe this meaning, all other meanings will be thoroughly understood and deeply believed without doubt.

blocks.text: Section Twenty-Two: No Dharma Can Be Attained

inline.s: (Ji) Third, clarifying that no Dharma can be attained. This has two parts: (Wu) first, declaring the awakening; next, confirming and explaining.
(Wu) First, declaring the awakening.
Subhūti said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, when the Buddha attained anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, was it then that nothing was attained?”

Above, first, in terms of merit and virtue, he spoke of its unreality. “Unreal” serves to clarify that what is condition-arisen is empty in nature. Nothing exceeds the adorned reward-body in the greatness of merit and virtue; hence next, in terms of the perfection of bodily marks, he clarified emptiness of nature. The manifesting of these bodily marks was originally for the sake of speaking Dharma; hence third, in terms of the speaker of Dharma having no Dharma that can be spoken, he clarified emptiness of nature. Speaking Dharma was originally for the sake of saving living beings; hence fourth, in terms of living beings, he clarified emptiness of nature. Each layer presses one step further. Pressed to this section, it is empty all the way through, like a barrel with its bottom fallen out. Why do I say this? The Buddha manifests the perfect bodily marks originally in order to speak Dharma and save living beings; and what the Buddha speaks is originally the speaking of what he has attained — what is called speaking according to suchness. Now we know that none of it is other than condition-arisen. What is condition-arisen is empty in its very substance. Hence the perfect bodily marks are named yet unreal; speaking Dharma too is named yet unreal; living beings too are named yet unreal. Then is it not that attainment is no attainment, that Buddha is no Buddha, that throughout all is named yet unreal? Then not a thread hangs on one, and the nature of empty stillness is revealed in its entirety. This is the essential purport of this section.

The Elder said earlier: in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, the Buddha had no Dharma by which he attained anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. Yet he still thought this referred to the time of the eighth ground, when, because he did not hold to a Dharma of bodhi, he now became Buddha and attained bodhi. Now he knows that what is called the Buddha’s attainment of bodhi is likewise an attainment without anything attained. The meaning is deeper than before. Hence, declaring his first awakening, he speaks the one word “was it then?” — precisely revealing the sight of one emptiness to the very bottom, like waking from a dream. This is said in terms of the matter. Spoken in terms of principle, the Elder had long been mind-to-mind with the Tathāgata; that he now declares a first awakening is precisely to point out to students that they should investigate to the very bottom in this way, not allowing a single thread of dharma-clinging to remain, so that afterwards self-emptiness becomes evident, initial enlightenment joins original enlightenment, and great enlightenment is accomplished. That he deliberately puts it as a question is again to point out to students that although they awaken thus, they should request a clear-eyed person to certify it. The first sentence speaks first of the Buddha’s attaining anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi; this clarifies that spoken in terms of cultivating the cause and realizing the fruit, it is not ultimately no attainment. The second sentence only then says “nothing attained”; this clarifies that spoken in terms of Dharma, it is not ultimately attainment. Taken together, they clarify the meaning of attaining the unattained, of attaining yet not attaining. There is an eye in these sentences; they must not be taken loosely.
(Wu) Next, confirming and explaining.
“Just so, just so, Subhūti. In anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi I have not even the least Dharma that can be attained; therefore it is named anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

Saying “just so” twice confirms that the words above — not ultimately no attainment, not ultimately attainment — are a correct awakening. What the Buddha says goes deeper: he presses the Elder’s words back to their source. It is as if to say, why is nothing attained? Because originally there is not the least Dharma that can be attained. This meaning directly continues from the word “I.” That I have not the least Dharma that can be attained precisely clarifies that I am empty. Because I am empty, I do not even see the least Dharma — how could there be the least Dharma attained? And since there is not the least Dharma attained, how could there be a Buddha who attains Dharma? The words “not even” precisely clarify that it is emptiness upon emptiness, all swept away together. At that very moment, not one thought arises; clear and still, the virtue of the nature is perfect and bright. In short, within the empty stillness of nature there is fundamentally no least Dharma. To see the least Dharma is precisely self-view; what attainment could there then be? Only in that one does not see the least Dharma that can be attained is there true attainment.

The sentence says that in supreme bodhi I have not the least Dharma that can be attained — how wondrous! It is that I do not see the least Dharma that can be attained. Beneath the words is the sense that it is not that there is ultimately no Dharma; hence he continues, “therefore it is named anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi,” revealing that there is not nothing of the name and word of supreme bodhi. He further reveals that supreme bodhi is but a name and word — how could one cling to it? Hence there is not the least Dharma that can be attained. He further reveals that what is called Dharma and what is called attainment are both produced by causes and conditions. What is condition-arisen is empty in substance. At the very moment there are such names and words, there is originally not the least Dharma that can be attained. The glance darts in four directions, and it is subtle on all eight sides. The meaning that came before — that no Dharma can attain bodhi — here pours forth with nothing left out; and so the meaning that no Dharma can produce bodhi is thereby thoroughly penetrated as well. This is precisely to open the bodhisattva’s right knowing, so that he may penetrate no-self and no-Dharma.

Above, the section on the mind’s activity being ungraspable dispelled the grasping subject; the section on all dharmas being condition-arisen dispelled the grasped object. Yet subject and object stand against each other and draw in more and more. Hence within the grasped dharmas there is again subject and object. For instance, merit and the surpassing reward are what is produced; the six pāramitās of giving are what produces. And in terms of the dharma of giving: the Dharma is what is given, the speaker is the one who gives. In terms of the affair of giving: the speaker of Dharma is the one who gives, the living beings who hear the Dharma are what is given. To distinguish still more finely: the self is what realizes, the Dharma is what is realized. In short, no affair is other than a standing-against; where there is standing-against there is subject and object; where there is subject and object there is discrimination; where there is discrimination there is clinging. And the least discrimination is the sixth consciousness, what is called the mark of self; the least clinging is the seventh consciousness, what is called self-view. Hence he clarifies one by one that all of them are condition-arisen, so that one may know that what is condition-arisen is empty in substance, named yet unreal, and that one must step by step contemplate emptiness and layer by layer dispel them. The reason he painstakingly dispels the dharmas on the object side is precisely in order to painstakingly dispel the self on the subject side; for the two are formed by standing against each other, and when one dissolves the other dissolves too. But to speak first of the mind’s activity being ungraspable is to dispel directly on the subject side. Yet the mark of self and self-view are not easy to dispel; they are mostly moved by outer objects. Hence he speaks of all dharmas in greater detail. From this one may know the method of applying effort. To dispel the subject one should dispel the object; to dispel the object is to dispel the subject. To dispel subject and object is to dispel discrimination; to dispel discrimination is to dispel clinging. When discrimination is wholly dispelled, the sixth consciousness turns; when clinging is wholly dispelled, the seventh consciousness turns. Once the two consciousnesses have turned, self and Dharma are both empty, and all is one suchness. All being one suchness is what is called equality. Hence the next words, “this Dharma is equal,” directly reveal the substance of the nature.

blocks.text: Section Twenty-Three: Purifying the Mind and Practicing Goodness

inline.s: (Ren) Next, concluding revelation. This has three parts: (Gui) first, directly revealing the substance of the nature; next, precisely pointing out the work of cultivation; third, concluding that there is no subject or object.
(Gui) First, directly revealing the substance of the nature.
“Again, Subhūti, this Dharma is equal, without high or low. Therefore it is named anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

This section of concluding revelation is the confluence of all the meanings spoken above. Everything said above — whether principle, whether affair, whether nature, whether cultivation — a thousand threads and ten thousand strands, all come to rest in these few lines. The various meanings are like a net; these few lines are the net’s main cord. Once the main cord is lifted, the mesh opens. Hence if the meaning of these few lines can be thoroughly comprehended in one’s breast, all the meanings can be threaded through and one knows how to apply them. If not, then though one hears many meanings, one still feels them fragmentary and scattered, like loose sand. And if the principle has not been grasped in its essentials, how could the work of cultivation seize the essentials? The bearing of this section is thus great indeed. That it should be received with wholehearted attention goes without saying.

“Again” separately raises one meaning in order to clarify the preceding meaning. What is said below all explains the reason why bodhi has not the least Dharma. Hence the two words “again” mark it out. The two lines “this Dharma is equal, without high or low” directly reveal supreme bodhi. Yet the two words “this Dharma” absolutely must not be pinned down to bodhi — nor is it only the two words “is named” that should not be pinned down. Why? The purport of the sutra is precisely to dispel the clinging to reality of those who cling to bodhi. Moreover, what is clarified here is precisely the reason why bodhi has not the least Dharma; how could the two words “this Dharma” be pinned down and explained as supreme bodhi? If pinned down and explained so, would that not make bodhi possess a Dharma? Even the New Eye Commentary cannot escape this fault.

Only the two commentaries of Master Sengzhao and Master Zhiyi are best. Their comment says: “Persons have no noble or base; dharmas have no fair or foul; utterly level and equal — this is the meaning of bodhi.” That is to say, when all notions of fair and foul, noble and base, unequal and unlevel, are utterly emptied, then it is level and equal. This itself is the meaning of bodhi. This explanation both makes clear that it is precisely bodhi and yet does not pin it down; it is thoroughly reasonable and wondrously accords with the sutra’s purport. From this one may know that “this Dharma” means whatever Dharma it may be — it is as if to say all dharmas.

“Without high or low” precisely reveals its equality. You should know that the reason all dharmas appear high or low is the false view of living beings’ discrimination and clinging, which sees them so. In truth the nature of all dharmas is equal, equal — how could there be high or low? And since there is no high or low, how could there be a Dharma of supreme bodhi? Hence he says, “therefore it is named anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.” For there being no way to name it, this name is provisionally set up. That is why bodhi has not the least Dharma that can be attained. If supreme bodhi had the least Dharma, then since it is called supreme, the marks of high and low would stand out plainly — how could that be the nature of equality? The Buddha’s becoming Buddha is precisely because he realized the equal dharma-nature. Hence it is said, “Tathāgata” means the meaning of suchness of all dharmas. Hence he sees all dharmas as Buddha-Dharma. Hence the anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi that the Tathāgata attains is therein neither real nor unreal. Why? Because where all dharmas are one suchness, this Dharma is equal; because all dharmas are Buddha-Dharma, there is no high or low. Since the dharma-nature is equal and one suchness, what is there to attain? Hence “neither real.” And just when there is not the least Dharma that can be attained, the equal and one suchness of the dharma-nature is perfectly revealed. Hence “nor unreal.”

You should know that where there is no high or low, all standing-against is cut off; with no standing-against, it becomes absolute; hence it is provisionally named supreme. With no high or low it is equal; hence it is provisionally named rightly equal. Why is it thus equal with no high and no low? Because it differs from ordinary beings, who, unawakened, set up discrimination and clinging at random. Yet there is no division of an awakener and an awakened either. Hence it is provisionally named right enlightenment. From this one may know that precisely because he does not discriminate dharmas, does not cling to dharmas, and does not even keep the view of dharmas, he is named supreme, rightly equal enlightenment. That he has not the least Dharma is clear. The dharma-nature is originally thus; the Buddha merely reveals this original nature. That he has not the least attainment is clear. Hence he says: in anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi I have not even the least Dharma that can be attained.

The former half causes one to not abide in any dharma, dispelling the discriminating self-clinging — all to reveal the equal nature. The latter half causes one not to abide even in the Dharma of bodhi, dispelling the innate self-clinging — also all to reveal the equal nature. When he has explained the meaning that all dharmas are suchness, he further uses the meaning of ungraspability to empty the mind that grasps, and uses the meaning of condition-arising to empty the dharmas that are grasped. When subject and object are both empty, the substance of the equal nature is revealed. Hence the section is titled “directly revealing the substance of the nature.” It can be seen that what is called the Dharma of supreme bodhi is nothing else: it is the equal nature of all dharmas as one suchness. If there were the least shadow of a Dharma of bodhi, how could one see the nature? Why? The substance of the nature is empty and still, and therefore equal. With the least discrimination or clinging, something is set up — how could there still be empty stillness? With the least thing set up, high and low appear — how could there still be equality? A bodhisattva should penetrate this principle and wholly dispel discrimination and clinging, so as to be without self. What is called the nature of all dharmas being originally without high or low — the things before one’s eyes are all like this; alas that living beings do not know how to contemplate. Suppose there is a thing or an affair here: one may see it as delightful, another may see it as loathsome, yet the thing or affair is not different according to the person. This suffices to show that the nature of all dharmas is originally without high or low. For the difference of delight and loathing lies in the persons; it has nothing to do with the thing.

Hence the man of many sorrows is nowhere without sorrow; though he meets a state that need not be sorrowed over, he still locks his brows in sorrow. The seeker of pleasure is never not pleased; though there is nothing to be pleased about, he still forces a smile. The environment is the same, yet what people feel differs in ten thousand ways — because what they see differs. Take water again as an illustration. A human sees it as water; fish and dragons see it as a dwelling; asuras see it as weapons; hungry ghosts see it as pus and blood. The sutra says this is brought about by the power of karma. You should know how the power of karma produces these differences: precisely because the self-views of discrimination and clinging were each different at the outset, the karma they created differed. As for the two vehicles’ wisdom-eye, it sees that water is fundamentally empty and that there is not even water. The bodhisattva’s Dharma-eye not only sees that it is fundamentally empty but also sees the various differing marks and affairs of water. Thus although the various views differ, water itself is originally without such divisions of high and low. The Buddha-eye sees one suchness. “One suchness” means that the nature of water is fundamentally empty, and so it manifests marks of clear or turbid according to conditions; yet though it manifests all marks of clear and turbid, the nature of water is still fundamentally empty. All dharmas are like this. This is what is meant by “this Dharma is equal, without high or low.” You should know that what is called equality is not to cut down the high to make it low nor to raise up the low to make it high. That is precisely the false view of discrimination and clinging, which makes it still more unequal and still more unlevel; the more one seeks equality, the more confused it becomes. When the Buddha speaks of equality, he means to remove discrimination and remove clinging, letting things be high or low as they will while equality remains as it is. For once the mind is level and the mind is equal, then although marks and affairs have high and low, they go on being high and low, each following its own measure, not disturbing one another; and then all is equal. This is the true meaning of equality. Therefore one who admires the way of equality should begin by leveling his own mind and equalizing his own mind.
(Gui) Next, precisely pointing out the work of cultivation.
“By means of no-self, no person, no being, and no life, cultivating all good dharmas, one then attains anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

The preceding section has already, by “this Dharma is equal, without high or low,” directly revealed the substance of the nature. And this substance of the nature is inherently complete in everyone, lacking in none. But because of deluded conceptualizing (that is, discrimination) and clinging, it cannot be realized. (This cites a complete sentence from the Lotus Sutra.) That the Buddha appears in the world for the sake of one great causal matter is precisely for this one great causal matter; and that the Buddha speaks this sutra is likewise for this one great causal matter. From the opening of the sutra onward, a thousand words and ten thousand phrases, spoken sideways and spoken upright, layer after layer peeled away, layer after layer washed clean — all for the sake of washing clean one original face and bringing it out, so that the great assembly may recognize it. Once recognized clearly, one knows that unless one truly cultivates in earnest according to all the meanings spoken above, one cannot realize it. For although the substance of the nature is inherently complete, it has been defiled by discrimination and clinging and is no longer the original face. Unless the mind of high and low and the view of inequality are wholly removed, how can the original be seen?

Yet what the sutra says is on the page; it is not one’s own. Now if one wishes to set out on a journey, one cannot but open one’s eyes; and opening the eyes is precisely for the sake of setting out. If one does not set out, what are the opened eyes for? Hence, having said the eight words “this Dharma is equal, without high or low,” directly displaying the substance of the nature so that the great assembly may open their eyes and recognize it, he at once points out precisely the work of cultivating and realizing it, so that the great assembly may set out and thus reach the goal. If one would make the whole of cultivation consist in the nature, one must arouse cultivation from the whole of the nature. That is why this sutra presses and unfolds layer upon layer, insisting that one profoundly understand the purport of the meaning. And when it reaches the preceding section, it still more directly reveals the substance of the nature so that the assembly may recognize it — truly fearing that they may fail to understand profoundly and mistakenly take the mind of birth and death as the cause of their cultivation. That the ancients, in cultivating, first had to awaken to the original nature was for this reason; and the chief reason the ancients attained the Way in greater numbers than people today lies precisely here.

In accordance with the principle stated above, all the work of cultivation spoken of in this section takes its start directly from “this Dharma is equal, without high or low.” Why do living beings see high and low in all dharmas? For no other reason than discrimination and clinging. Discrimination is the mark of self and other standing against each other; clinging is self-view. Hence they see high and low and are unequal; hence they are at odds with the substance of the nature. That is why this sutra, as soon as it opens its mouth, causes the arousing of the vast mind and the subduing of the marks of self and others. “By means of” means using. To use no-self, no person, no being, and no life is to say, using a mind without discrimination or clinging. “Good dharmas” is the giving spoken of above. To name one giving is to include the six pāramitās; the six pāramitās include the ten thousand practices. Hence “all good dharmas.” To say “by no-self cultivating all good dharmas” clarifies that whatever Dharma it may be, equal, equal, one must with this equal mind contemplate all dharmas and cultivate as occasion requires, not harboring a mind of high and low. These two lines joined are precisely the meaning stated when the sutra opened: “one should give while dwelling on nothing.” To dwell on nothing is to use a mind without discrimination or clinging. Abiding is clinging. Where there is clinging there is discrimination; as soon as there is discrimination, there is clinging. The two matters arise together in correspondence and are not apart. “Giving” is precisely what is meant by cultivating all good dharmas.

The line “by no-self” is emptiness, not clinging to existence — cultivating wisdom. The line “cultivating all good” is existence, not clinging to emptiness — cultivating merit. Thus the two wheels run together, which is again not clinging to either extreme; then it perfectly accords with the middle way, equal, equal, and corresponds to the equal nature of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. Hence “one then attains.” “One then attains” means one certainly attains. “Attains” means realizes. If we analyze it: cultivating all good dharmas with a mind free of discrimination and clinging accords with the meaning that all dharmas are suchness — the cause of accomplishing the dharma-body. Adorning both merit and wisdom — the cause of accomplishing the reward-body. Perfectly cultivating all and gaining the wisdom of skillful means — the cause of accomplishing the transformation-body. Since it is a perfect cultivation according with the nature, the virtue of the nature is perfect and bright, the three bodies appear, and supreme, rightly equal enlightenment is accomplished. Hence “one then attains.” This states in sum the meaning that the whole nature arouses cultivation and the whole of cultivation consists in the nature. The meaning of “by no-self and so on cultivating all good dharmas” includes the meanings of the earlier phrases: “one should not grasp Dharma, one should not grasp non-Dharma,” as well as “one should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing” and “one should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing.” The phrases “are not” and “is named” all serve to unfold this meaning. “One then attains supreme bodhi” is likewise the meaning of the earlier saying, “when the mind of faith is pure, then true marks arise.” Nor is that all. The very first section, on arousing the mind apart from marks, which is subduing, causing the arousing of the vast vow — this is precisely causing one to cultivate all good dharmas by means of no-self, no person, no being, and no life. (Read the former phrase again.) Next, the section saying that not abiding in marks is right abiding, causing the practice of the vast practice — this too is precisely causing one to cultivate all good dharmas by means of no-self, no person, no being, and no life. (Read the latter phrase again.) The whole sutra text in fact takes the first two sections as its main theme; everything spoken afterwards is either an exposition of that theme’s principle and substance, or a revelation of its cultivation and purpose, or an analysis of its hidden subtleties, or an unfolding of its final purport.

Broadly, the former half first causes one not to abide in any dharma amid the conditions of objects, as in what is said before the request for the name and its upholding. After that, it causes one not to abide in any dharma at the moment of giving rise to mind and moving thought — and it has been speaking more and more urgently. The latter half, at its opening chapter, causes one not to abide even in the Dharma of supreme bodhi when giving rise to mind and moving thought; everything said afterwards is devoted to dispelling this one point. When it says the mind of the three periods is ungraspable, it makes one know that what grasps is an ungraspable deluded thought, not the true mind. It further says all dharmas are condition-arisen, making one know that no dharma is other than at once provisional and at once empty; when the ten thousand appearances are arrayed in profusion, they are at once utterly ungraspable. Even the Buddha’s reward-body and the Dharma of bodhi he realized are all illusory existents, all utterly ungraspable. Long ago the Second Patriarch of Chan asked the First Patriarch to reveal the Dharma of pacifying the mind. The First Patriarch said: “Bring me your mind, and I will pacify it for you.” The Second Patriarch was at a loss for a long while, then said: “I seek the mind and it is ungraspable.” The First Patriarch said: “I have finished pacifying your mind for you.” What does it mean that the mind was already pacified? Truly, because living beings’ permanently abiding true mind had long been disturbed into confusion by what is ungraspable, not knowing that it is entirely due to their own discrimination and clinging, which keeps them grasping without rest and so forms the mark of confused turmoil; this is what is meant by “taking the mind to grasp the mind, and what is not illusion becomes the Dharma of illusion.” If one knows that the mark of confused turmoil is fundamentally ungraspable and absolutely does not grasp it, then at that very moment one is cool and clear. Hence, “I have finished pacifying your mind for you.” This is just so too. When not the least Dharma of bodhi is to be found, then face after face of every dharma is bodhi. Why seek elsewhere? Hence he directly reveals bodhi by the two phrases “this Dharma is equal, without high or low.”

How can this equal bodhi be revealed? It comes from the extinguishing of both subject and object spoken of above. How are subject and object both extinguished? It comes from the arousing of the vast vow and the practice of the vast practice spoken of when the sutra opened. Having aroused the vast vow, one does not grasp Dharma. (Because one arouses the vow to save without the mark of saving, one does not grasp Dharma.) Having practiced the vast practice, one does not grasp non-Dharma. For to grasp either Dharma or non-Dharma is to cling to self, person, being, and life. Since Dharma and non-Dharma are both ungrasped, self, person, being, and life — these four — are all absent. Since the four are absent, Dharma and non-Dharma are utterly ungraspable; likewise the mind of the three periods of discrimination and clinging is utterly ungraspable; likewise the cultivating and the cultivated, even the realizing and the realized, are utterly ungraspable. Since all these are utterly ungraspable, one plainly and clearly attains the permanently abiding true mind, what is called “this Dharma is equal, without high or low.” This is the earlier saying, “when the mind of faith is pure, then true marks arise.” This is what is meant by “by no-self, no person, no being, and no life, cultivating all good dharmas, one attains anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.” In short, these three lines of sutra text are the concluding meaning of all the phrases spoken since the sutra opened, so that one may grasp this essential outline and thereby penetrate all that has been said above; they do not set forth a separate meaning apart from all that has been said above. One should blend and contemplate them thus.

Moreover, from what has been said above, it is evident that this sutra speaks of practice in affairs from its very first word; all the various principles and natures afterwards are spoken on the basis of practice in affairs. To speak of principle and nature without departing from practice in affairs is the essential knack of teaching Dharma. Why? Because “to make emptiness evident within the existent” is precisely not clinging to either extreme. These four words, “to make emptiness evident within the existent,” encompass the whole purport of prajñā. Keep them firmly in mind, my friends, and practice accordingly, and you will naturally accord with the middle way. What is said here, “by no-self cultivating all good dharmas,” also carries this meaning. That is to say, when cultivating all good dharmas one should be without self. If one does not cultivate all good dharmas and yet calls it no-self, that is most perilous. Why? Because it is either an evil grasping at emptiness or a one-sided emptiness. You should know it thus.
(Gui) Third, concluding that there is no subject or object.
“Subhūti, what are called good dharmas, the Tathāgata says are not good dharmas; therefore they are named good dharmas.”

Supreme bodhi cannot be clung to as real. How then can all good dharmas be clung to as real? If one clings to them as real, how is that different from clinging to supreme bodhi as real? Hence they too must be dispelled. All good dharmas are nothing but condition-arisen provisional existents, at once existent and at once empty. Hence, spoken according to the meaning of suchness, all good dharmas are at that very moment “not.” There is only a provisional name — how could one cling to them as real? Hence he says: “the Tathāgata says they are not good dharmas; therefore they are named good dharmas.”

Above he said, “by no-self cultivating all good dharmas,” which dispels on the side of what cultivates. Here he says, “not good, named good,” which dispels on the side of what is cultivated. If there is a Dharma that is cultivated, there is a thought that cultivates. Where there is object and subject, there is plainly the mark of standing-against, which is discrimination and clinging. With the subtlest discrimination remaining, the mark of self still remains; with the subtlest clinging remaining, self-view still remains. Hence they must be dispelled to the very end. You should know that “by no-self and so on cultivating all good dharmas, one then attains supreme bodhi” is because one cultivates with a mind free of discrimination and clinging; hence one attains bodhi. For cultivating with this equal mind, Dharma is then no Dharma, and in the cultivating there is no longer a cultivator or a cultivated. Cultivating without cultivating, one can then attain without attaining. Hence what this section says is a matter simultaneous with the arousing of cultivation — that is, when cultivating all good dharmas, one contemplates “not good, named good.” If in one’s mind one sees good dharmas, that is precisely self-view; how then can it be called cultivating all good dharmas by no-self and so on? In other words, this section precisely explains the reason for the words above, “no-self, no person, no being, and no life”; it does not say that after cultivating all good dharmas one dispels them again. It absolutely must not be seen as two separate pieces from the preceding section. You should know it thus.

Looking at what has been said above, we may know that this section of concluding revelation is not only the concluding revelation of this section’s setting forth of fruit and clarifying cause; it is the concluding revelation of all the meanings since the sutra opened. In other words, all the meanings spoken since the sutra opened are nothing but “by no-self cultivating all good dharmas, so as to realize the equal nature” — and only here is this pointed out plainly.

The first two sections of this sutra, on arousing the vast vow and practicing the vast practice, set forth the meaning at the opening of the chapter. Counting roughly afterwards, there have already been several concluding revelations. The first is the two lines, “one should not grasp Dharma, one should not grasp non-Dharma.” The second is the passage, “one should thus give rise to the pure mind.” The third is the long passage, “one should be apart from all marks and resolve for bodhi.” The fourth is the long passage on all dharmas being of the meaning of suchness, neither real nor unreal, all being so. Now this is the fifth. And the five, before and after, have their own order of shallowness and depth.

The first, the two lines, concludes the meaning that saving living beings is not abiding in marks and giving is not abiding in marks. Not abiding in marks is not grasping Dharma; giving and saving living beings is not grasping non-Dharma. The second is the concluding revelation that one who widely practices the six pāramitās should dwell on nothing, in order that emptiness and existence both be ungrasped, and the self-nature’s pure mind, empty according to suchness and not empty according to suchness, may come before one. The third concluding revelation clarifies that only apart from marks is it resolving for bodhi; not only does one not cling to either extreme, one should not cling even to non-clinging. Hence: “one should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing; where there is abiding, it is not so,” and so on. The fourth concluding revelation, in terms of the fruit, shows the state of one who has realized the pure mind: it is a state in which not one dharma abides, in which every dharma is suchness, in which there is no self. It makes one know that all the meanings spoken above are nothing but causing not one dust to stand and wholly dispelling the subtlest discrimination and clinging, so that one may realize what the Buddha realized. This fifth concluding revelation plainly reveals that the nature of all dharmas is originally equal, without high or low; hence not one dharma may be discriminated or clung to. The Dharma of bodhi is so, and all good dharmas are so too. One has only to use a mind free of discrimination and clinging to cultivate all good dharmas that are without high or low, equal, equal — and one then accords with the dharma-nature and sees the original face of stillness and illumination at once. The five, before and after, are not disordered by so much as a hair in their order of shallowness and depth; moreover every drop returns to the source — the utmost in fineness and detail, the utmost in perfect interfusion.

blocks.text: Section Twenty-Four: Merit and Wisdom Beyond Compare

inline.s: (Xin) Third, revealing the surpassing and concluding with exhortation. This has two parts: (Ren) first, introducing a simile to reveal; next, the proper conclusion and exhortation.
(Ren) First, introducing a simile to reveal.
“Subhūti, if someone took the seven treasures gathered in measure equal to all the Mount Sumerus, kings of mountains, in a great trichiliocosm, and gave them away…”

Within one great trichiliocosm there are a thousand million Mount Sumerus, kings of mountains. Gathered together, the seven treasures would be as many as these. “So” refers to that thousand million. To take such an amount of seven treasures and use it for giving — that gift may be called surpassing, and the greatness of the merit may be known. This section introduces a simile in order to reveal that the merit of receiving, upholding, and widely speaking this sutra, as set out below, is still greater.
(Ren) Next, the proper conclusion and exhortation.

“If someone receives, upholds, and speaks for others this Prajñā Pāramitā Sutra, even so much as a four-line verse — the merit of the former giver does not come to a hundredth part of it, nor to a hundred thousand myriad millionth part, nor can it be reached by reckoning or by simile.”

The circulating editions read “receives, upholds, reads, and recites.” The original text has no words “reads and recites,” for these are included within “receives and upholds.” “Than the former merit” — “than” carries the sense of comparison. “Former” refers to the giver of seven treasures equal to a thousand million Mount Sumerus mentioned above. The sense is: the merit of the former giver may be called great; yet by a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a ten-thousandth part, a hundred-millionth part of that merit, or even by a part that reckoning cannot reckon or simile cannot liken, none can come up to a single part of the merit of one who upholds and speaks this sutra. For though the sutra is but words and names, from words contemplation arises, and from contemplation one goes on to resemblance, to partial realization, and at last to the full accomplishment of supreme bodhi. How could any merit with marks compare with it?

When the former half was concluded, it plainly said it would not speak in full. Hence the latter half’s comparison revealing the surpassing is seen only now for the first time. Yet the intent of this comparison is again quite different in flavor from the earlier ones. You should know that this section is spoken after the direct revelation of the substance of the nature. To reveal the substance of the nature is to reveal the dharma-body. Earlier he used Mount Sumeru, king of mountains, as a simile for the reward-body; now, however, he has one give away seven treasures gathered in measure equal to a thousand million Mount Sumerus, kings of mountains, and yet that merit falls far short of upholding and speaking this sutra. The sense is that upholding and speaking the sutra can cause self and others alike to realize the dharma-body; compared with that, the reward-body is like wealth outside the body — how could it be worth measuring? You should know that the Buddha’s manifesting the reward-body and so on is originally for the benefit of living beings, to give them something to enjoy — just as giving wealth in charity gives others something to enjoy. Hence he uses this as a simile to reveal that one who has realized the dharma-body does not abide even in the marks of the reward-body.

(Geng) Next, exhausting non-abiding to the utmost so as to accomplish realization. This has two parts: (Xin) first, clarifying the equal dharma-realm and revealing the accomplishment of the no-self of dharmas; next, clarifying the empty marks of all dharmas and concluding that dharmas are unborn.

This is the fourth great division. (Counting the whole sutra, it is the fourth division; but in terms of the latter half alone, it is the second division.) All of it speaks of the Tathāgata’s realm; hence “exhausting to the utmost.” It means that the investigation of non-abiding reaches its utmost here. What is called realization is the realizing of this. This fourth division on exhausting to the utmost is further opened into two: the first, clarifying the equal dharma-realm, serves to reveal that the nature of all dharmas is originally without self, and thereby to conclude the meaning of the preceding section, that a bodhisattva penetrates the no-self of dharmas. The next, clarifying the empty marks of all dharmas, comes to rest in neither arising nor ceasing. All that has been said since the sutra opened, causing one to be apart from marks and apart from thought in order to remove self-clinging, is nothing but the dispelling of discrimination and clinging — and discrimination and clinging are what is called the mind of birth and death. To dispel the mind of birth and death is to realize the substance of the nature that neither arises nor ceases. This is the final gathering point of the whole deeply profound prajñā. Hence the main body of the teaching ends here — that is, the thirty-first division of Prince Zhaoming; its thirty-second division belongs to the circulation section.

(Xin) First, again three parts: (Ren) first, clarifying in terms of saving living beings that there is no sage or ordinary being; next, clarifying in terms of nature and marks that they are neither one nor different; third, concluding no-self in terms of not receiving merit and virtue.

These three sections all closely follow the meaning that this Dharma is equal. The intent is to teach those who hear the Dharma that in every dharma and at every point they should take up the principle of equality, and then in every dharma and at every point they may see the self-nature. The first section, clarifying that there is no sage and no ordinary being, precisely reveals that there is no high or low. In the one true dharma-realm, equal, equal, how could there be a distinction of sage and ordinary being? This meaning is most conveniently explained in terms of saving living beings; hence he clarifies it in terms of saving living beings.

blocks.text: Section Twenty-Five: Transforming Without Any Transformation

inline.s: (Ren) First, again two parts: (Gui) first, clarifying that saving is without the thought of saving; next, clarifying that there is originally no sage or ordinary being. (Gui) First, again two parts: (Zi) first, marking out; next, explaining and establishing.
“Subhūti, what do you think? You should not say that the Tathāgata gives rise to this thought: I should save living beings. Subhūti, do not give rise to such a thought.”

The gist of this section is the same as that of the earlier section on no Dharma that can be spoken. The only difference is that the former was spoken in terms of the Dharma spoken, while this is spoken in terms of the living beings saved. Yet speaking Dharma was originally for saving living beings, and saving living beings requires speaking Dharma; hence the gist is the same. All the meanings cited earlier from the ten-fascicle Sutra of Golden Light, explaining the reason the Buddha does not give rise to thought, apply here as well. In short, that the Buddha can save living beings without giving rise to mind or moving thought, responding to capacities and conditions, comes down to two principles. (1) Because the power of the seeds perfumed by his former great compassion and great vows enables him to respond wherever there is a sense of feeling. (2) Because he possesses the two knowledges and has accomplished the three bodies, like a great perfect mirror whose light illumines everywhere, he can respond without error.

Possessing these two principles, he differs from ordinary beings, who must give rise to thought whenever they do anything. “Do not give rise to such a thought” is a universal admonition to everyone, not spoken solely to the assembly then present. For to give rise to such a thought is to measure the sage’s realm by ordinary sentiment. Not only does one slander the Buddha; one also remains deluded in the nest of deluded conceptualizing, with never a hope of becoming a sage. Hence he earnestly admonishes against it. In short, the words “do not give rise to such a thought” not only forbid measuring the ocean of perfect enlightenment with the view of saṃsāra; they truly require that a student of the Buddha’s teaching must cut off deluded thought. When the sutra opened it at once caused the bodhisattva to subdue this thought, hence: “in truth there is no living being who attains extinction.” The latter half likewise says at its opening that not one living being has actually attained extinction. Now he again speaks in terms of the Buddha’s saving living beings, so that all bodhisattvas may take it as their standard.

Although the text above twice said that living beings are not living beings, that was spoken of living beings alone. Here, however, he speaks of sage and ordinary being together, to clarify the equal dharma-realm; the meaning differs from before. Someone may say: the Lotus Sutra states, “When I first sat at the place of enlightenment, I gazed at the tree and also walked in meditation; for twenty-one days I pondered such matters as this. The wisdom I attained is subtle, wondrous, and foremost; living beings’ faculties are dull, blinded by attachment to pleasures and by delusion. Beings such as these — how can they be saved?” From this it is evident that there plainly are sages and ordinary beings; why then say there is no sage or ordinary being? Moreover, the Buddha pondered in detail both the saving of living beings and the Dharma he would speak before he spoke it. Pondering is thought; why then does this sutra say there is no thought? You should know that where there is sage and ordinary being, this is spoken in terms of marks; where there is no sage or ordinary being, this is spoken in terms of nature. That is why this sutra says “are not” and also says “is named.” As for the meaning of pondering, I should explain it in two layers to forestall doubt.

(1) Of all that the Buddha speaks, some is spoken according to what is fitting, which is called provisional teaching, also called incomplete meaning. Some is spoken in the ultimate sense, which is called true teaching, also called complete meaning. The sentences quoted above from the Lotus Sutra are provisional teaching spoken according to what was fitting. For he observed and knew that all living beings, dull-facultied and blinded by delusion, are attached to the pleasures of the five desires, and cannot correspond to the pure wisdom and subtle Dharma the Buddha realized. Beings such as these — how could they be saved? Hence, as a last resort, he first taught the three vehicles, from the shallow to the deep. Yet in teaching the three vehicles he was in truth teaching the one vehicle — what is called opening the provisional to reveal the real. Here this sutra is precisely clarifying the equal dharma-realm, and all its sentences are ultimate and according-to-suchness statements; hence its sentences are mostly spoken joined to the two words “Tathāgata.” “Tathāgata” means the meaning of suchness of all dharmas. What is suchness? True suchness. What is true suchness? The state apart from thought. How could one cite the provisional to prove the true teaching? Moreover, what is called provisional is itself provisional in and of the real. Hence although it says “pondered,” in truth it is pondering yet no pondering. In reading Buddhist sutras, the first thing to understand is this meaning. Even the Buddha constantly calls himself “I” — how could one, because of his accommodating expression, say the Tathāgata has the mark of self and self-view?

Again, this sutra sets forth this supreme and deeply profound Dharma, yet the Buddha puts on his robe and begs for food, appearing just like an ordinary being. How could one, on that account, doubt that the Buddha is an ordinary being? The Elder everywhere asks questions on behalf of living beings — how could one take him dully and say the Elder truly did not understand prajñā? In the world many doubt whether Avalokiteśvara is male or female. Now a great being of the dharma-body is fundamentally without marks; whatever body he manifests is entirely a response to capacities and conditions. As it is said, for whatever body is fit to be saved, he manifests that body and saves them. The Śūraṃgama and Lotus sutras explain this meaning in detail. How could one regard him as an ordinary being and fix him as male or female? Even speaking of the great being’s past causes: through many kalpas of diligent cultivation, what body did he not have? And how could one take the body of a single lifetime to cover the bodies of many kalpas? Matters of this kind in the Buddhist sutras, and sentences that contradict each other, are very many indeed; all should be understood in this way.

(2) “Pondering” means contemplating. Contemplation is also translated as the cultivation of pondering. The two verses from the Lotus Sutra quoted above (four lines make one verse) come in continuation of the line above them, “I contemplated with the Buddha-eye.” What the two verses say is, in sum, that he contemplated living beings’ capacities. You should know that at the time of contemplation there is neither no-thought nor thought. One who knows contemplation even a little can understand this state clearly; it is utterly different from brooding and deluded conceptualizing. How could one mistake pondering for giving rise to thought? In short, that there are living beings to save and a Dharma to speak is spoken in terms of marks. The Buddha’s performing this contemplation is precisely what is called stillness yet constant illumination. Yet at the very moment such marks and affairs appear, they are at once utterly ungraspable. Hence he also says there is no Dharma that can be spoken and no living being to save — that is spoken in terms of nature. Though he contemplates, there is nothing contemplated: illumination yet constant stillness. Hence if one takes the two Lotus verses quoted and joins them with what is said here, it is precisely the meaning that nature and marks are perfectly interfused, stillness and illumination simultaneous; and it is the meaning that the provisional is of the real, and the real is of the provisional. One should penetrate it thus. If one clings to one and doubts the other, one clings to marks and doubts nature, clings to nature and doubts marks, clings to stillness and doubts illumination, clings to illumination and doubts stillness. This is precisely the ordinary being’s knowing and seeing — what is called dull faculties blinded by delusion, incapable of corresponding to the wisdom that is subtle and foremost. Hence a student of the Buddha’s teaching must open the Buddha’s knowing and seeing. The Buddha’s knowing is knowing that all is ungraspable, knowing that all is at once empty and at once provisional. The Buddha’s seeing is not clinging to one or different. To cling to one and doubt the other is precisely to cling to oneness and difference. Hence if one would penetrate the subtle wondrous principle of Buddha-Dharma, unless one sweeps ordinary sentiment and worldly views utterly away, one can by no means enter.
(Zi) Next, explaining and establishing.
“Why is this? In truth there is no living being whom the Tathāgata saves. If there were a living being whom the Tathāgata saves, then the Tathāgata would have self, person, being, and life.”

“In truth there is no” pauses briefly; these two words are thoroughgoing. They mean that in truth there is no such reason for giving rise to thought. What is meant by “in truth there is no such reason”? The meanings are many; let me speak briefly of four.

(1) If there were a thought of saving living beings, there would be living beings saved and a self that saves. Subject and object are the marks of standing-against; that is discrimination, that is clinging. The Buddha realized the equal one true dharma-realm, and hence is called Tathāgata. If he had discrimination and clinging, how could he be named Tathāgata? Hence to say the Tathāgata gives rise to such a thought — in truth there is no such reason. This clarifies the meaning in terms of the equal dharma-realm, and is also spoken from the Tathāgata’s side.

Let me speak again from the side of living beings. (2) What are living beings? Nothing but a coming-together of the five aggregates. This is a condition-arisen dharma, and what is condition-arisen is empty in substance. If there were a thought of saving living beings, would that not be failing to understand condition-arising and clinging to the dharmas of the five aggregates as truly existent? Where there is clinging to dharmas, there is clinging to self. Could the Tathāgata have the two clingings of self and Dharma? Hence to say the Tathāgata gives rise to the thought “I should save living beings” — in truth there is no such reason. This clarifies the meaning in terms of what is condition-arisen being empty in substance.

(3) The reason living beings become living beings is that they have thought. The reason living beings are saved is that they are without thought. Hence what is called saving living beings is only causing them to be apart from thought.
