If the Buddha had a thought in saving living beings, then he himself would not yet be saved — how could he save living beings? Hence to say the Tathāgata gives rise to the thought “I should save living beings” — in truth there is no such reason. This clarifies the meaning in terms of being apart from thought being what is called saving.

(4) The Buddha’s saving of living beings is nothing but an augmenting condition for living beings; it is living beings themselves who arouse the great mind and practice the great practice, and this is truly the primary cause. Without the primary cause, even with the augmenting condition there would be no way for living beings to be saved. Hence when living beings are saved, it is truly living beings saving themselves. That the Buddha does not have this view is the Buddha’s saving of living beings. Hence to say the Tathāgata gives rise to the thought “I should save living beings” — in truth there is no such reason. This clarifies the meaning in terms of the cause being intimate and the condition being distant.

Gathering these four meanings: as for there being living beings whom the Tathāgata saves, the Buddha truly has no such thought. This sentence explains the reason straightforwardly. After the word “if,” he again speaks in reverse to explain the reason. “There is” means there is thought. If there were this thought, one would fall into subject and object. What saves is the mark of self; what is saved is the mark of person; that what is saved is not only one person is the mark of being; that this thought continues without interruption is the mark of life. If there is a single thought, the four marks are complete. The Tathāgata is precisely causing bodhisattvas who have aroused the mind to remove these four marks; yet to say the Tathāgata has the four marks would be to slander the Tathāgata most extremely. Hence he earnestly admonishes, “do not give rise to such a thought.” Here he is precisely refuting the wrong statement that the Tathāgata gives rise to such a thought. Hence he clarifies only from the Tathāgata’s side (that is, the first of the four meanings stated above) the meaning that there is no subject, no object, and no self, the intent being to cause students to understand clearly that in the equal dharma-realm there is truly no self.
(Gui) Next, clarifying that there is originally no sage or ordinary being.
“Subhūti, when the Tathāgata says ‘I,’ then there is no I; yet ordinary people take it as an I. Subhūti, ordinary people — the Tathāgata says they are not ordinary people.”

The circulating editions mostly have the line “therefore they are named ordinary people.” The Tang manuscript sutras, the Southern Song canon, and the commentaries of the ancient worthies all lack it; it most certainly should not be there.

This section explains why there is no one who saves and nothing saved. As for the word “I” here, if one takes it merely as the “I” of self and person, that is of course not unacceptable, but the meaning would be shallow. You should know that the word “I” directly continues the “I” of “I should” above, and refers to the Buddha’s own words. “I” is then no I, revealing that in the equal dharma-realm the Buddha is no Buddha — precisely clarifying that there is no sage. For the title “Buddha” reveals his realization of the fruit; the title “Tathāgata” likewise reveals his realization of the nature. The one true dharma-realm is apart from names and cuts off marks — how could it have such names? Moreover, the one true dharma-realm is another name for the nature shared in common by all Buddhas and all living beings. Because it is shared in common, it is called one suchness; hence it is called equal, without high or low. If the word “Buddha” were in it, there would be high and low, and it would not be equal; there would be name and mark, and it would not be empty stillness. Hence, spoken according to the meaning of suchness, what is called having a Buddha or a sage is then not having a Buddha or a sage. It is only ordinary people, who know only how to grasp marks and do not penetrate the one true dharma-realm, who suppose there is a Buddha or a sage. In the equal dharma-realm, the Buddha himself does not remain — how could there be anyone who saves or any Dharma that can be spoken? And since it is equal and shared in common, there is not only no sage — how could there be an ordinary being? Hence what is called an ordinary person, spoken according to the meaning of suchness, is then not an ordinary person. The ordinary itself does not remain — how could there be anything saved that can be spoken of? No high, no low, equal, equal — this is what is meant by the substance of the nature being one suchness. (This suffices to show that later people who rashly added the line “therefore they are named ordinary people” were truly gilding the lily.)

No sage, no ordinary being — this is precisely the reason there is no high or low; hence it is called equal. The substance of the nature is originally thus equal. Therefore the Buddha says that above there is no Buddha-way to accomplish and below there are no living beings to save. For saving is no saving, and accomplishing is no accomplishing. Hence it is said: the equal true dharma-realm — the Buddha does not save living beings. Hence the Buddha-eye sees all living beings as originally Buddhas. All of this is spoken in terms of the substance of the nature being equal.

Why does he speak of the meaning of equality? In order to cause bodhisattvas who have aroused the mind to penetrate this meaning: they should, with a mind of no subject, no object, no Dharma, and no self, cultivate all good dharmas, and only then can they thus realize it. From this one may know that although a cultivator should arouse the vow to turn from ordinary being and become sage, once the vow is aroused he must at once set aside the thought of ordinary being and sage. If he does not set it aside, sage and ordinary are forever separated. Why? That the sage becomes sage and the ordinary becomes ordinary is precisely because one is without thought and the other has thought; as soon as thought arises, there is high and low, and it is not equal. The ancients, in instructing cultivators, had one sentence that is best of all: “Just go straight on.” “Straight on” means with never a backward glance. The cultivator need only understand the principle clearly and fix his direction, and then go straight on. Whether he turns from ordinary or not, whether he becomes sage or not, and all matters of life and death, gain and loss, and so on — he does not hang his mind on any of them. In this way he accords with the Way and accords with the nature, and can quickly accomplish it. Otherwise he cannot accomplish it at all. The ancients had another warning line: “Let the incense burner of the old shrine go cold” — meaning that all thought should be ashes and cold. When one does not hang one’s mind even on sage and ordinary, one may know the rest.

blocks.text: Section Twenty-Six: The Dharma-Body Is Not Marks

inline.s: (Ren) Next, clarifying in terms of nature and marks that they are neither one nor different. This has two parts: (Gui) first, generally revealing the meaning of suchness; next, separately dispelling emotional clinging.
(Gui) First, generally revealing the meaning of suchness.

“Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be contemplated by means of the thirty-two marks?” Subhūti said: “Just so, just so — the Tathāgata may be contemplated by means of the thirty-two marks.”

This section, clarifying in terms of nature and marks that they are neither one nor different, is a crucial guiding eye of the whole sutra, and its meaning is deep and subtle; without dissecting it layer by layer, it is not easy to understand clearly.

“Contemplating” differs from “seeing.” Spoken in terms of the Tathāgata manifesting a body, it is “seeing”; spoken in terms of a student cultivating contemplation, it is “contemplating.” The sense of the question is: can one contemplate the response-body that has marks and thereby contemplate the dharma-body that is without marks? One has marks, one is without marks — of course it cannot be. Yet the response-body is originally manifested from the dharma-body, and the “without” of “without marks” is not ultimately nothing. What is called true marks is “no marks yet not no marks.” Thus it is not after all impossible. Nevertheless, if one clings to it as possible, one unavoidably grasps marks and falls into the fault of clinging to existence. Hence below there follows the section first dispelling the grasping of marks to clarify that they are not one. But if one clings to it as impossible, one unavoidably annihilates marks and falls into the fault of falling into emptiness. Hence below there further follows the section dispelling the annihilation of marks to clarify that they are not different. Consider the Elder’s answer: it can add considerably to one’s insight. And to hear further what the Buddha dispels opens the eye of the mind all the more. You should know that from the opening of the sutra onward, layer upon layer of dispelling, with the repeated saying “are not” and “is named,” is nothing but guarding students against clinging to one side. Here, clarifying that nature and marks are neither one nor different, is precisely explaining the reason one should not cling to one side.

“What do you think?” is a phrase that tests and examines one’s insight. He has tested it repeatedly before; that he tests it again now is because here he does not say “see” but “contemplate.” The sense of the question is extremely fine, quite different from before. For he fears precisely that students, hearing that all dharmas are of the meaning of suchness and that this Dharma is equal, may be vague and muddled, unable to enter deeply into the subtle, and yet suppose themselves to be one suchness and equal. Then an error of a hairsbreadth becomes a mistake of a thousand miles. Hence he must test and examine them again, and reveal it to them.

Before giving the answer, there are two essential meanings that must first be clarified. (1) At the prajñā assembly, the Buddha had the Elder teach the bodhisattvas in turn (see the Great Prajñā Sutra). This shows that the Elder had long been mind-to-mind with the Buddha; the purport of prajñā he had long known deeply. That in this sutra he deliberately appears not to know is in order to request the Dharma on behalf of living beings. (2) The deeply profound principle is fundamentally beyond speaking. Now, as a last resort, within the unspoken he speaks it. One person at one time cannot say two different things; hence he entrusts it to two people and sets it out in the form of question and answer, so that the deeply profound purport may be somewhat more easily made evident. In accordance with these two meanings, what the Elder says is no different from what the Buddha says. In all sutras, the person who is the fitting recipient should be regarded in this way — not only in this sutra. This is an essential meaning and must not be unknown.

If the phrase “just so, just so” is taken merely as a word of assent, one not only belittles the Elder but also leaves the deep purport contained in the sutra unshown and obscured. How would one belittle the Elder? Consider: the first time the Buddha asked, “Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of bodily marks?” the Elder at once answered that bodily marks are no bodily marks. The second time he asked, “Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks?” he again answered, “are not” and “is named.” The third time he asked, “Can the Buddha be seen by means of the perfect bodily form? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the perfect marks?” — to both he answered that one should not. Why does he here suddenly cling to marks like this? The Elder is of course representing living beings, yet to be clear and then suddenly muddled does not accord with principle. Hence the phrase “just so” is truly not a word of assent; it is a statement of principle.

“Such” is the meaning of suchness of all dharmas. “So” is “all is so.” Did he not say earlier that in the former half there is not a single answer of “just so,” while in the latter half wherever he answers “just so” it expresses a subtle meaning? For instance, in clarifying the five eyes, every answer is “just so”: this clarifies that the flesh-eye is not fixedly a flesh-eye, and so on up to the Buddha-eye not being fixedly a Buddha-eye. In short, five are not fixedly five, one is not fixedly one — one must not cling to one. This is precisely what is meant by all dharmas being one suchness and all being so. The sense is that only where there is suchness is all so; where there is no suchness, all is not so. Hence every answer is “just so.” Next, when asked whether the Ganges’ sands are spoken of, he also answers “just so”: this clarifies that the Tathāgata’s saying the sands of the Ganges is a saying according to the meaning of suchness, not the same as an ordinary person’s saying. Again, when asked about merit and causal conditions, he also answers “just so”: this clarifies that every dharma is condition-arisen, and that if one realizes that what is condition-arisen is empty in nature, then every dharma is suchness and every dharma is so. Hence the next line: “this person, by these causal conditions, gains merit and virtue beyond measure.” The sense is that only because it is condition-arisen can great merit be attained; and only because it is condition-arisen should one not cling to the marks of condition-arising, but converge into the nature of one suchness. Then although every dharma is condition-arisen, every dharma is also Buddha-Dharma. Elsewhere he does not answer “just so.” Here, answering “just so” again carries the same sense as before; and that he says it twice is to make people take the word “such” seriously — one must be able to be such, and only then is one so.

The sense is that the thirty-two marks are also one of all dharmas. All dharmas are true suchness — how could the thirty-two marks not be true suchness? But one must realize the meaning of suchness, and only then is it so. Why? If one comprehends that nature and marks are one suchness, then one neither annihilates marks nor clings to marks; and so contemplating the response-body of the thirty-two marks is contemplating the Tathāgata’s dharma-body. If one goes against the meaning of suchness, one will inevitably either cling to marks in order to contemplate the nature, or else annihilate marks in order to contemplate the nature — and then nothing is right. “Just so, just so — the Tathāgata may be contemplated by means of the thirty-two marks” should be read as one sentence. It states in sum that, in accordance with the meaning of suchness, to contemplate the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks is right. The Elder’s sense is that contemplating differs from seeing. When in the mind one forms the contemplation of the thirty-two marks, it is fundamentally the mark of no mark; and the Tathāgata’s manifesting the thirty-two marks is likewise marks that are no marks. Now, understanding that mark of no mark and forming the contemplation, one neither grasps marks nor annihilates marks — precisely according with the meaning that true marks are no marks yet not no marks, and precisely according with the meaning of suchness of all dharmas, and precisely according with the Tathāgata. Hence: “Just so, just so — the Tathāgata may be contemplated by means of the thirty-two marks.” The sense is that since it is already one suchness, contemplating marks is contemplating the nature.

The Elder’s answer is truly deeply profound, truly perfectly complete, truly corresponding to the Buddha’s intent. Yet the Tathāgata below still further refutes and dispels it. For although the Elder’s clarification of the meaning of suchness is right, there remains within it a subtle principle that must be recognized clearly and distinguished plainly. Otherwise one will inevitably become vague and muddled, taking what one has not seen for seeing, and mistaking a donkey’s saddle-girth for grandpa’s chin. This meaning is truly crucial, for it is what students most easily blur. Hence the Buddha and the Elder, one asking and one answering, make evident this hidden and subtle deep purport, so that students may not mistake it.

(Gui) Next, separately dispelling emotional clinging. This has two parts: (Zi) first, dispelling the grasping of marks to clarify that they are not one; next, dispelling the annihilation of marks to clarify that they are not different. (Zi) First, again two parts: (Chou) first, refuting and explaining, revealing and dispelling; next, speaking a verse to conclude.
(Chou) First, refuting and explaining, revealing and dispelling.

The Buddha said: “Subhūti, if one contemplates the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks, then a wheel-turning sage king would be a Tathāgata.” Subhūti said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, as I understand the meaning the Buddha has spoken, the Tathāgata should not be contemplated by means of the thirty-two marks.”

The Buddha’s sense is: when you say “just so, just so — the Tathāgata may be contemplated by means of the thirty-two marks,” at first hearing it is quite right. Yet if the source and ground are not clearly recognized, I fear it may be plausible but wrong. Why? The thirty-two marks are by no means manifested by the Tathāgata alone; a wheel-turning sage king possesses them too. Yet the wheel-king’s marks come from karmic merit, unlike the Tathāgata’s, which are manifested from the dharma-body. Now if one hastily and vaguely says, “Just so, just so — the Tathāgata may be contemplated by means of the thirty-two marks,” then the wheel-king would also be a Tathāgata — is that not a great error? You should know that the Buddha’s words indeed speak of the marks contemplated, but his intent is truly to reveal the one who contemplates. For the wheel-king, whose karmic consciousness is not yet empty, also has the thirty-two marks because of karmic merit. This suffices to show that marks are all illusory and not to be relied upon. But if the contemplator’s karmic consciousness is already empty, then not only can the wheel-king’s thirty-two marks not deceive him; even when he contemplates the five-aggregate bodily form of a living being, he can see through to the dharma-body and does not see the five aggregates. If it is not so, then even face to face with the Tathāgata he contemplates only marks and cannot see the dharma-body.

The Buddha says this precisely because one who has just aroused the mind and is cultivating contemplation has not broken through so much as a hairsbreadth of ignorance and is still within karmic consciousness. If such a one hears the teaching that all is one suchness and that this Dharma is equal, and without weighing his own measure hastily says that contemplating marks is contemplating the nature, he does not know that what he contemplates is precisely consciousness and not the nature. All students should examine this carefully.

How should one examine it? (1) The ordinary being of the broad earth, from beginningless time, since unawakened and moving of itself, has long had nature and marks not one. Why not one? Because of grasping marks. Why grasp marks? Because of karmic consciousness. Hence one must wholly empty all marks and cut off emotional consciousness before one can speak of nature and marks being one suchness. (2) The Buddha’s speaking of the meaning of suchness is to cause one to recognize the one true dharma-realm, to remove discrimination and clinging, and to be without self. Hence one should examine oneself: am I discriminating? am I clinging? If there is the subtlest discrimination or clinging, that is karmic consciousness — how can one say that contemplating marks is contemplating the nature?

In short, one suchness and equality can be brought to its ultimate only by the Buddhas. One must neither cling to the real nor let even illusory marks remain, until not one thought arises and even “not arising” is absent — only then is it one suchness and not different. Hence what is called all dharmas being one suchness is to see only the nature of one suchness and not to see the marks of the dharmas. Nor is that all: it must be that although there is one suchness and equality, there is also no such thing as one suchness and equality — only then is it true one suchness and true equality. How could one whose karmic consciousness is not yet empty rashly take it upon himself? Now, to say “contemplate the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks” plainly keeps a contemplator and a contemplated; that is discrimination and clinging, and karmic consciousness is plainly there. Yet he says, “just so, just so.” He does not realize that it is already not such, and not so in the least. Through the ages how many cultivators, when their coarse thoughts have somewhat subsided, say they have already realized samādhi; with habitual tendencies still present, they say they are at ease and soaring. All such confuse the muddled with the perfectly interfused, and few do not fall. Reading this sutra text is truly a sharp needle driven into the crown of the head.

What the World-Honored One refutes, the Elder had already clearly understood; hence he turned as soon as the opportunity came. And his earlier answer was likewise spoken in anticipation of living beings’ disease; that is why he made his words vague, waiting for the World-Honored One to refute them, so that all living beings might examine and refute themselves and not fall into confusion.

Wherever the phrase “Subhūti said to the Buddha” is marked, it always shows an intent of solemnity; the same is so here. The intent is to cause students not to read this refutation carelessly. “Understanding the meaning of what is spoken”: having heard and known that the wheel-king shares the same marks and that marks are not to be relied upon, one understands that for all dharmas to be one suchness, one must wholly dissolve all marks and only then can it be. The Elder understands it thus, precisely to cause students to understand it thus. “Should not”: the sense is that it is not absolutely impossible — if one’s emotional consciousness is already empty, then having marks is equal to having no marks, and having no marks is no obstacle to having marks. But it is not for one who still has the least emotional consciousness to blur. Hence “should not.” These words are precisely a keen admonition to students.

In short, the Buddha’s speaking of one suchness and equality is to cause one to be unable to cling either to oneness or to difference. Now, to contemplate the nature by means of marks plainly clings to oneness. Can one still say it is one suchness?
